subject: music
title: Reading Rhythm
welcome_lead: Practice clapping the rhythms you see.
meta_desc: KS3 notation: reading and clapping rhythm patterns.
final_note: Once you can read it, you can play it.

concepts.def: Pattern of long and short notes.
Curved line joining notes into one longer.
Dot adds half the note's value.
Three notes in time of two.

walkthroughs.body_html: In 4/4 say '1-2-3-4' aloud, evenly. For quavers add 'and': 1-and-2-and-3-and-4-and. Tap your foot on the numbers.
A tie joins two notes into one longer note. A dot after a note adds half its value — a dotted crotchet = 1.5 beats.
A triplet squeezes three notes into the time of two. Marked with a small '3' above. Used to give a swingy, jazzy feel.

A triplet is three notes in the time.

mcqs.q: Which chords form a plagal cadence?
options: ii to V.
IV to I (the 'amen' cadence).
It is always C major.
V to I.

mcqs.q: What is a balanced antecedent-consequent phrase?
options: ii to V.
A long melody with no breaks.
Two phrases of equal length where the first sounds open (question) and the second resolves (answer).
Any two phrases of similar style.

mcqs.q: How do you identify a major key from its key signature?
options: It is always C major.
The number of sharps or flats equals the tonic note number.
ii to V.
The last sharp is the leading note (semitone below tonic); the second-to-last flat is the tonic.
